title: IsPQGroup: Bundled pq-Group Hypothesis
content: `IsPQGroup G` is a structure bundling all hypotheses about a group of order pq: the two primes `p` and `q`, their primality proofs `hp`, `hq`, distinctness `hpq`, and the cardinality `hcard : Fintype.card G = p * q`. By packaging these as a structure, every theorem in the file can take a single `h : IsPQGroup G` argument rather than six separate hypotheses, keeping theorem statements clean and focused. The private helper lemmas (`factorization_pq_at_q`, `sylow_q_card`, `sylow_q_index`, etc.) use this structure to derive that Sylow subgroups have orders exactly $p$ and $q$ and indices $q$ and $p$ respectively — the key facts for the counting arguments.
mathContext: For $G$ with $|G| = p \cdot q$ (distinct primes), the p-adic valuation $(p \cdot q)_{(p)} = 1$, so the Sylow $p$-subgroup has order $p^1 = p$ and the Sylow $q$-subgroup has order $q^1 = q$. Their indices are $q$ and $p$ respectively by Lagrange.

title: Unique Sylow q-Subgroup: n_q = 1 for All pq-Groups
content: `sylow_q_count_constraint` extracts the two Sylow III constraints on $n_q$: it divides $p$ (the index of any Sylow q-subgroup, derived from `sylow_q_index`) and $n_q \equiv 1 \pmod{q}$ (from `card_sylow_modEq_one`). `unique_sylow_q` then closes the argument: if $n_q \geq 2$, by primality of $n_q \mid p$, either $n_q = 1$ (done) or $n_q = p$; but $n_q = p$ implies $p \equiv 1 \pmod{q}$, i.e., $p \% q = 1$; since $p < q$, $p \% q = p$, so $p = 1$, contradicting $p$ prime. The key arithmetic step is `Nat.mod_eq_of_lt hpq : p % q = p`. `sylow_q_normal` wraps the result.
mathContext: $n_q \mid p$ and $n_q \equiv 1 \pmod{q}$, with $p < q$: if $n_q = p$, then $p \equiv 1 \pmod{q}$, so $p = 1 + kq \geq q + 1 > p$ for $k \geq 1$, impossible. Hence $n_q = 1$.

title: Sylow p-Subgroup Analysis: n_p ∈ {1, q} and the Coprimality Criterion
content:
`sylow_p_count` uses that $n_p \mid q$ (prime) so by primality $n_p \in \{1, q\}$. `unique_sylow_p_when_coprime` shows that if $p 
mid q-1$, then $n_p 
eq q$: if $n_p = q$, then `card_sylow_modEq_one` gives $q \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$, i.e., $p \mid q-1$, contradicting the hypothesis. The key Mathlib bridge is `Nat.modEq_iff_dvd'`: $q \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ iff $p \mid q - 1$ (valid since $1 \leq q$). `both_normal_when_coprime` packages both results to give two normal Sylow subgroups when $p 
mid q-1$.
mathContext: $n_p \mid q$ (prime) so $n_p \in \{1, q\}$. $n_p = q \Rightarrow q \equiv 1 \pmod{p} \Rightarrow p \mid q-1$. Contrapositive: $p \nmid q-1 \Rightarrow n_p = 1$.

title: Core Cyclicity Proof: Commutator Argument and Order Product Formula
content: `cyclic_of_both_sylow_normal` is the 80-line original proof. Step 1 (disjointness): the commutator argument relies on $P \cap Q = \{1\}$, proved by showing any $x$ in both has order dividing both $p$ and $q$; by coprimality of $p$ and $q$, `Nat.eq_one_of_dvd_coprimes` gives $\text{ord}(x) = 1$. Step 2 (commutativity): for $g \in P$, $k \in Q$, the commutator $[g,k] = g^{-1}k^{-1}gk$ is simultaneously in $P$ (by normality of $P$: $k^{-1}gk \in P$, and $g^{-1} \in P$) and in $Q$ (by normality of $Q$: $g^{-1}k^{-1}g \in Q$, and $k \in Q$). Since $[g,k] \in P \cap Q = \{1\}$, we get $g$ and $k$ commute. Step 3: generators of cyclic-prime-order groups P and Q commute, so `Commute.orderOf_mul_eq_mul_orderOf_of_coprime` gives $\text{ord}(gk) = p \cdot q = |G|$. Step 4: `Subgroup.zpowers(gk) = ⊤` via `Subgroup.eq_top_of_card_eq`.
mathContext: $P \cap Q = \{1\}$ (coprime orders). $[g,k] \in P \cap Q = \{1\} \Rightarrow g, k$ commute. Then $\text{ord}(gk) = \text{ord}(g) \cdot \text{ord}(k) = p \cdot q = |G|$, so $G = \langle gk \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}/pq$.

title: Classification Theorem and Concrete Examples
content:
`nonabelian_sylow_p_count` characterizes non-cyclic pq-groups: if $p \mid q-1$ and $G$ is not cyclic, then $n_p = q$ (by contradiction: $n_p = 1$ would force both Sylow subgroups normal, then `cyclic_of_both_sylow_normal` gives $G$ cyclic). `pq_cyclic_classification` is the main exported theorem: for any group of order $pq$ with $p 
mid q-1$, $G$ is cyclic. The four concrete `omega`-proved examples confirm the arithmetic: order 15 ($3 
mid 4$, only $\mathbb{Z}/15$), order 35 ($5 
mid 6$, only $\mathbb{Z}/35$), order 6 ($2 \mid 2$, also $S_3$), order 21 ($3 \mid 6$, also non-abelian).
mathContext: The complete classification: $|\text{Groups}(pq)| = 1$ if $p \nmid q-1$ (only $\mathbb{Z}/pq$), $|\text{Groups}(pq)| = 2$ if $p \mid q-1$ ($\mathbb{Z}/pq$ and $\mathbb{Z}/q \rtimes \mathbb{Z}/p$). Orders 6, 10, 14, 15, 21, 22, 26, 33, 34, 35, 38, ... are covered by this theorem.
